0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
The message. Jude is a fire-bell. Teachers have slipped into the church who turn God’s grace into a licence for sin and deny Jesus Christ by the way they live, and Jude calls believers “to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (v. 3). He shows from Scripture that God has always judged such people, then tells the faithful how to stand and how to rescue those being drawn away. Many Christians know only the closing doxology, but it belongs with all that comes before it. The letter opens with a people who are “kept for Jesus Christ” (v. 1) and closes with God, who is “able to keep you from stumbling” (v. 24). Between those two words about God’s keeping, Jude describes the darkness without flinching.

Background: the writer. The author calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). The James everyone knew was James the brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9), and Mark lists a Judas among Jesus’ brothers (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55). So the writer is most likely Jude, who grew up in the same house in Nazareth as Jesus. During Jesus’ ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). After the resurrection they are found praying with the apostles (Acts 1:14), and later the Lord’s brothers travelled as missionaries (1 Corinthians 9:5). Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early church, yet he calls himself a slave of Jesus Christ. Before Easter he had a brother; after Easter he had a Lord who had once been his brother. An early story preserved by Eusebius tells of Jude’s grandsons, poor farmers, questioned under the emperor Domitian and released when they showed their work-hardened hands.

Did Jude really write it? Some scholars think a later writer used Jude’s name. But anyone borrowing a name for authority would hardly choose so little-known a figure, and then not even call him the Lord’s brother. Some early churches hesitated over the letter, partly because it quotes 1 Enoch, but by the end of the second century it was widely received as Scripture. This commentary takes it as the work of Jude the brother of Jesus. The date is uncertain. If Peter drew on Jude, as seems likely, it was written before the mid-60s, probably in the 50s or early 60s.

The first readers. Jude names no place. His readers knew the Old Testament well and also the Jewish traditions about Enoch and about Moses’ burial, so they were probably Jewish Christians, perhaps in Palestine or Syria, or churches where Jewish believers set the tone. The intruders had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4). They were probably travelling teachers living on the hospitality of house churches. At the church’s “love feasts” (v. 12), the shared meals at which believers also kept the Lord’s Supper, they were “hidden reefs”, rocks under calm water. They claimed visions, “relying on their dreams” (v. 8); they treated grace as permission for sexual sin (vv. 4, 7–8); they scorned authority and the unseen powers (vv. 8–10); they flattered the influential for gain (v. 16) and divided the church, while themselves “devoid of the Spirit” (v. 19).

The letter he did not write. Jude had meant to write warmly about “our common salvation” (v. 3), but the danger was too pressing, and he wrote an alarm instead. Faithful ministry sometimes sets aside what we hoped to say for what the moment requires.

Jude and 2 Peter. Much of Jude reappears in 2 Peter 2: the angels who sinned, Sodom, Balaam, the pictures of dry water and storm-driven cloud, and the gloom of darkness reserved for the ungodly. Most scholars think Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it, and that is the more likely reading; some think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on common teaching. Either way, an inspired writer may use another’s words, as the prophets and apostles often did.

Jude and 1 Enoch. Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day (vv. 14–15), and draws on a tradition, perhaps from a lost work called the Assumption of Moses, about Michael disputing with the devil over Moses’ body (v. 9). Quoting a true saying does not make a whole book Scripture, any more than Paul’s quoting of pagan poets made them inspired; the canon is closed without 1 Enoch.

How the letter makes its case. Jude’s twenty-five verses form one sustained argument in four movements. First the greeting and the alarm: who the readers are, and why he must write (vv. 1–4). Then the evidence (vv. 5–16). Three examples show God judging those who had privilege and despised it: Israel saved from Egypt and then destroyed in the wilderness for unbelief, the angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 5–7). Then comes the portrait of the intruders, who rail where even Michael would only say, “The Lord rebuke you” (vv. 8–10); who walk in the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah (v. 11); who are reefs, waterless clouds, dead trees, wild waves and wandering stars (vv. 12–13); and whose judgment Enoch foretold (vv. 14–16). Again and again Jude says “these”, applying each old text to the people in front of him. Then he turns to the faithful (vv. 17–23): remember the apostles’ warnings; build yourselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, “keep yourselves in the love of God” and wait for Christ’s mercy; and show mercy to the doubting, snatching some “out of the fire” while hating the sin that clings to them. Last comes the doxology (vv. 24–25). Jude thinks in threes throughout: called, beloved, kept; mercy, peace, love; Israel, angels, Sodom; Cain, Balaam, Korah.

Where it leads: to Christ. The intruders deny “our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (v. 4), and the whole letter defends his right to rule his people. In the ESV’s reading of verse 5 it was Jesus “who saved a people out of the land of Egypt”, and other manuscripts read “the Lord”; either way, the Lord who rescued Israel and judged its unbelief is the Lord the church now serves. Enoch’s Lord who comes with his holy ones is, for Jude, most likely the risen Jesus coming to judge. Yet his people do not dread that day. They are kept for him (v. 1), and they wait “for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life” (v. 21). The God who will present them blameless is praised “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (v. 25): only through the Son can sinners stand before that glory with joy.

For us. Jude teaches the church to hold together two things it is tempted to separate: firm contending for the truth and deep mercy towards those who waver. False teaching rarely announces itself; it comes in smiling, at the church’s own table, and calls its looseness freedom. The answer is not suspicion of everyone but a people built up in the faith, praying, keeping themselves in God’s love, and pulling others from the fire. You can contend without bitterness, rescue others without being stained yourself, and hold on under pressure, because the One who keeps you is stronger than everything that threatens you. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration, and that adoration is the ground the whole letter stands on.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
Where we are. Jude has only one chapter, so this is the whole letter: a short, urgent alarm sent to churches into which false teachers had quietly crept.

The message. Fight for the gospel God has handed you once for all, because men inside the church are turning his grace into a licence to sin, and God has always judged such people; but fight as those whom God himself is keeping. Jude’s alarm is framed by two words about God: his people are “kept for Jesus Christ” (v. 1), and he is “able to keep you from stumbling” (v. 24). The danger is real and the judgment certain, but the safety of those who belong to Christ is more certain still. Jude warns in order to make his readers brave, not anxious: his is the courage of people who know they are held.

Why it was said. Teachers who claimed visions had found a welcome at the church’s love feasts, and they taught that grace made sexual sin and contempt for authority harmless (see the introduction). Jude had meant to write warmly about “our common salvation” (v. 3), but a church eating at the same table as such men needed a warning first.

How the chapter makes its case. After a greeting that tells the readers who they are (vv. 1–2), Jude states his purpose: contend for the faith, because ungodly men have slipped in (vv. 3–4). Then he gives the evidence. Three examples show God judging those who had privilege and despised it: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their place, and Sodom (vv. 5–7). The intruders repeat those sins (vv. 8–10), walk in the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah (v. 11), and are pictured as reefs, waterless clouds, dead trees, wild waves and wandering stars (vv. 12–13), whose judgment Enoch foretold (vv. 14–16). Then Jude turns to “you, beloved”: remember the apostles’ warnings (vv. 17–19), keep yourselves in God’s love by building, praying and waiting, and rescue the wavering with mercy (vv. 20–23). The doxology crowns it all (vv. 24–25). The darkness of verses 5–16 is framed by a people who are kept and a God who is able to keep them.

Where it leads. The intruders “deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (v. 4), and the whole letter defends his right to rule his people. He is the Lord who brought Israel out of Egypt (v. 5) and the Lord who will come with his holy ones to judge (vv. 14–15). Yet those who belong to him do not wait for that day with dread. They wait “for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life” (v. 21), and it is “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (v. 25) that stumbling sinners will stand blameless before God’s glory, with great joy.

For us. Jude calls us to hold together what we tend to separate: firm contending for the truth and deep mercy towards those who waver. Watch for any teaching that makes grace an excuse for sin; build your own life on the faith, in prayer and in God’s love; reach out to those who are drifting; and rest in the God who is able to keep you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are, because only people who know they are held can face danger bravely. They are called, summoned by God; beloved in God the Father, resting in his love now; and kept for Jesus Christ, guarded until he comes (v. 1). Then he prays that mercy, peace and love will be theirs in abundance (v. 2). Every alarm that follows is heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called, Beloved, Kept

The security of believers rests on God’s call, love and keeping, not on their own grip (see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church shaken by false teachers is first reminded of its security.

Now: A believer who fears drifting away begins where Jude begins (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude, the Lord’s brother who became his servant, greets the church as people God has called, loves and keeps, and prays that mercy, peace and love will be theirs in abundance.

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ. “Servant” (doulos) is slave: one whose will belongs to another. Jude grew up in the same house as Jesus, in a family that once thought him out of his mind and did not believe in him (Mark 3:21; John 7:5; see the introduction). Like James (James 1:1), the only other New Testament writer who could call himself the Lord’s brother, he does not mention it. This is not false modesty. Before Easter, Jude had a brother; after Easter, he had a Lord. To call himself the slave of Jesus is to confess that Jesus rose and that this changed everything: what matters now is not family but faith (Mark 3:35).

And brother of James. James was the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9). Jude names him to establish who he is, not to claim status.

To those who are called. Three descriptions of the readers follow. “Called” (klētois) is God’s call that actually brings a person to faith (Romans 8:28–30), his effectual call: God’s act, not their initiative.

Beloved in God the Father. “Beloved” (ēgapēmenois) is in a Greek tense that means loved and still loved. Before Jude says a word about danger, he tells them where they live: inside the Father’s unchanging love.

And kept for Jesus Christ. “Kept” (tetērēmenois) is the same tense: guarded and still guarded, as a treasure is kept for its owner, or a bride for her bridegroom. Their safety does not rest on their own hold; God is holding them.

Mercy, peace, and love. “Multiplied” (plēthyntheiē) is made abundant. In a letter about danger, Jude opens with what God gives: mercy that does not hold failures against them, peace that holds the heart steady, and love that holds them no matter what. Those who must contend need more of all three, not less.

The Father’s gift to the Son. Why would the Father keep a people for Jesus Christ? Because they are his gift to his Son, and it is the Father’s will that the Son should lose nothing of all that he has been given (John 6:37–39). The whole letter of warning is written to people the Father has promised his Son he will not lose.

In everyday life. Before you face anything hard today, a difficult conversation, a temptation, a worrying piece of news, say these three words to yourself: called, loved, kept. They are true of every believer: God did this for you, and it still holds today.

If I am kept, why does this letter warn me so strongly? Because warnings are one of the ways God keeps his people. A father who holds his child’s hand on a cliff path also says, “Stay away from the edge.” The warning does not mean he might let go; it is part of how he holds. So Jude tells you to keep yourselves in the love of God (v. 21), and then praises the God who keeps you (v. 24). Read every warning in this letter as the voice of the One who is guarding you.

Uncertain wording. “Kept for Jesus Christ” translates a plain dative (Iēsou Christō), which can mean kept for Jesus Christ or kept by him; older English versions have “preserved in Jesus Christ”. Most take it as “for”: the Father guards his people for the day his Son comes to claim them. Every reading leaves them safe.
verseByVerse.note: Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, came to faith after the resurrection. Much of his letter is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel has been handed to the church complete, and when it is attacked it must be defended. Jude meant to write a warm letter about “our common salvation”, but the danger forced him to write an alarm instead, calling believers to contend for the faith delivered once for all (v. 3). The reason: ungodly men have slipped in unnoticed, turning God’s grace into a licence for sensuality and denying Jesus Christ as Master and Lord (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
Contend for the Faith

On the faith once for all delivered, and the intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ, see the note on vv. 3–4.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jude set aside the letter he wanted to write because the danger was urgent.

Now: Contend as someone who loves the people being misled, not as someone who enjoys a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because ungodly men have slipped into the church, turning grace into licence and denying Christ’s lordship, believers must fight for the gospel God has handed them complete.

Our common salvation. “Common salvation” (koinēs sōtērias) is the salvation all believers share, Jew and Gentile, slave and free. Jude had planned a letter celebrating it, and it was never written. He is not a man who enjoys a fight but a pastor who would rather have celebrated; those who love the gospel most find it hardest to watch it distorted.

Contend for the faith. “Contend” (epagōnizesthai) is to fight earnestly, as an athlete strains in a contest; it is related to our word agony. “The faith” (tē pistei) is not personal trust here, but the body of truth believed, the gospel.

Once for all delivered. “Once for all” (hapax) is a single, final, complete delivery; “delivered” (paradotheisē) is handed down, entrusted like a precious deposit. The faith was given by God through the apostles, complete, and nothing may be added to it or taken from it (see “Where Christians differ” at the end of this note). It is their teaching about Christ: who he is, God and man; what he did in his life, his death for sinners, his resurrection and ascension; what he will do at his return and judgment; and how sinners are saved, by grace through faith, and called to holy lives. And it was delivered to the saints, not to an elite: every believer is entrusted with it.

Crept in unnoticed. “Crept in unnoticed” (pareisedysan) is slipped in sideways, like spies entering by a side door: gradually, plausibly, using the church’s own language. The most dangerous false teaching sounds like the gospel while quietly removing its foundations.

Long ago were designated for this condemnation. “Designated” (progegrammenoi) is written beforehand. Does it mean that God predestined these people to be condemned? Some read it so; but the word most naturally means written beforehand, and Jude’s examples that follow, Israel, the angels, Sodom and Enoch’s prophecy, suggest that the condemnation of such people was written in Scripture long ago. Behind that writing stands God’s sovereign rule of all things, so nothing about these men takes him by surprise. But their sin is their own: they perverted grace into sensuality, and they are justly judged for what they freely chose.

Ungodly people. “Ungodly” (asebeis) is irreverent, without regard for God, and it is a key word of Jude (vv. 4, 15, 18). They may be religious, but God is not feared in their lives.

Pervert the grace of our God. “Pervert” (metatithentes) is to change, turn into something else, and “sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained immorality. They twisted grace into a licence to sin, reasoning that since we are forgiven, sin does not matter (Romans 6:1–2). Any teaching that produces loose living rather than holiness has not understood grace; it has put something else in its place.

Our only Master and Lord. “Master” (despotēs) is a sovereign owner, and “Lord” (kyrios) the one who rules. In the Greek both titles belong to Jesus Christ, a strong statement of his deity: Master is the title the first believers gave to God himself in prayer (Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24). The intruders denied his lordship by their lives and perhaps by their teaching (Titus 1:16). To twist grace into permission to sin is already to deny him as Lord.

Nothing needs to be added. The faith was delivered once for all, because the Saviour did his work once for all: he lived the perfect life, died the one death that atones, rose and reigns, and nothing needs to be added. Over this grace stands our only Master and Lord, who bought his people and will not let them be stolen.

In everyday life. Take one central truth this week, for example the deity of Christ, justification by faith or the return of Christ, and learn to explain it simply with two or three Bible passages.

Shouldn’t a faith keep up with the times? Medicine and physics update themselves; why should belief be fixed in the first century? Every generation has its plan to keep the warmth of Christianity and quietly drop whatever the age finds embarrassing. But the updated versions date faster than anything, because they are married to one decade’s mood. G. K. Chesterton, in Orthodoxy, called tradition “the democracy of the dead”: it gives a vote to our ancestors and refuses to let the small minority who happen to be alive just now settle everything. A faith handed down once for all is the one thing that can stand outside our moment and question it. And the faith is not a theory waiting for better data; it is the report of a rescue God has carried out in Christ, and such a report does not grow less true with age. Every age needs not a newer gospel but the same Saviour: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

Does stressing grace not lead people to take sin lightly? Real grace never does. The grace that forgives also transforms: it unites us to Christ, gives us a new heart, and teaches us to say no to ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Those who use grace as an excuse show that they have not received it. The answer to the idea that Christians may ignore God’s law (antinomianism) is not less grace, as if the gospel needed a little law to keep people in line, but a true understanding of it. Those forgiven much love much, and love keeps God’s commandments (John 14:15).

How do I contend without becoming a contentious person? Contend for the faith, not for your preferences, and about what matters most: the person and work of Christ, the gospel of grace, the holiness it produces. Know your Bible well enough to do it. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), gently, without mockery, seeking to win people rather than defeat them. Distinguish between those who teach error and those who have been confused by it (vv. 22–23). And pray for those you disagree with. A contender who does not pray for his opponents has become a quarreller.

Where Christians differ: is the faith still developing through new revelation? Some churches hold that doctrine develops through ongoing revelation or the church’s teaching office, adding new dogmas over time; some charismatics expect new prophetic revelation, though many of them agree that it may never add to Scripture or overrule it, and they love the Bible as warmly as anyone. This commentary’s view: Jude says the faith was delivered once for all. The apostolic deposit is complete. The church’s understanding of Scripture may deepen, but no new doctrine may be added. Scripture alone is the final rule of faith, and the canon is closed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Privilege does not protect anyone who turns from God. Jude gives three examples his readers already knew. Israel was rescued from Egypt, yet the generation that would not believe died in the wilderness (v. 5). Angels stood in God’s presence, yet those who left their place are kept in chains for judgment (v. 6). Sodom had righteous Lot in its midst, yet its immorality brought a fire that still warns the world (v. 7). Each had unusual exposure to God, turned from him, and was judged.
verseByVerse.theology:
Privilege Is No Shield

Outward privilege is no substitute for persevering faith (see the note on vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers belonged to the church but were walking the same road as unbelieving Israel, the fallen angels and Sodom.

Now: The person most at risk is not the one who has never heard, but the one who has heard so often that the gospel has become background noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgments on unbelieving Israel, the rebel angels and Sodom show that no privilege shelters those who turn from him: the Lord who saves also judges.

I want to remind you. They knew these truths; they needed reminding (2 Peter 1:12). Like Peter, Jude believes the church’s great need is not novelty but memory.

Jesus, who saved a people. If “Jesus” is what Jude wrote (see the textual note below), Christ before he became man brought Israel out of Egypt, as Paul also implies (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9): the same Jesus opened the sea, fed them with bread from heaven, and gave them water from the rock that was himself. In either reading, salvation and judgment belong to the same Lord.

Afterward destroyed. “Afterward” (to deuteron) is literally the second time: first he saved, then he judged. Israel refused to trust the God who had brought them out of Egypt, and the generation aged twenty and over, except Caleb and Joshua, died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29–30; Hebrews 3:16–19). No privilege, the exodus then or baptism and church membership now, can take the place of persevering faith.

The angels. The second example. “Position of authority” (archē) is rule, rank, and “proper dwelling” (oikētērion) is home: heaven. These beings stood before God’s throne and walked out of his presence. Jewish tradition, especially 1 Enoch (a Jewish writing from the centuries before Christ, outside the Bible), linked this with the sons of God and the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4). Peter refers to the same angels (2 Peter 2:4).

Kept in eternal chains. A wordplay: they did not keep (tērēsantas) their position, so God keeps (tetērēken) them in chains. Believers are kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1); these angels are kept for judgment. High rank does not shield anyone from judgment; it makes them more answerable.

Sodom and Gomorrah. The third example: with Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23), they were the cities of the plain where Lot lived. “Likewise”: like the angels, they crossed boundaries God had set (see “Uncertain wording” below).

An example. “Example” (deigma) is a sample, a display. The cities of the plain became a permanent warning sign, and the fire that fell on them a sample of the eternal fire of the final judgment (Matthew 25:41), which is still coming. And yet the same Jesus came down to bear judgment for those who believe, so that the fire they deserved fell on him instead.

Does this mean that the saved can perish? Israel as a nation was brought out of Egypt, but the generation who did not believe died in the wilderness: outward deliverance and membership among God’s people are not the same as saving faith. Some read the example as a warning that true believers may be lost; more likely it warns professing believers not to trust in privileges without faith. Jude has just called believers kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1), and he will praise the God who is able to keep them from stumbling (v. 24).

Who are these angels? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning. Many Jewish and early Christian readers, and many today, link them with the sons of God of Genesis 6:2, pointing to Jude’s next words, that Sodom “likewise” sinned sexually. Calvin and many Reformed writers read those sons of God as the godly line of Seth, and some as kings. This commentary leaves the question open, as Genesis 6 does; the point stands either way: God judges rebellion and rescues his own.

If these angels are in chains, why are demons still active? Jude speaks of a particular group confined until the judgment, not of all fallen angels; others are still at work under God’s restraint (Ephesians 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8).

What was the sin of Sodom? Ezekiel names pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49), and Genesis shows the men of the city demanding sex with Lot’s visitors (Genesis 19:5). Jude names sexual immorality and desire against the created order. The passage agrees with the rest of Scripture that same-sex sexual practice is sin, among the other sins of a proud and godless city. The clearest passages are Leviticus 18:22, Romans 1:26–27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9–11, read in the light of God’s pattern for marriage as one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), which Jesus himself reaffirmed (Matthew 19:4–6).

I experience same-sex attraction, or love someone who does. What does this mean for us? It means you are not a special category of sinner; every believer battles disordered desires, and temptation itself is not sin. The call is the same for all Christians: to deny ourselves, take up the cross and follow Christ in holiness, which for every unmarried believer means chastity. The church must welcome, love, befriend and support such believers, not shame or isolate them. And for anyone who has fallen, 1 Corinthians 6:11 stands: such were some of you, but you were washed. Christ receives all who come.

How can a loving God punish for ever? Because sin is not a small offence against a small god but rebellion against the infinitely holy and good Creator, and those who persist in rejecting him go on rejecting him. Hell is God giving people, justly, what they chose: life without him, which is darkness. We must not soften what Jesus himself taught more than anyone. But the God who will judge has done the most costly thing imaginable to rescue us: he sent his Son to bear the fire in our place. Hell is not a reason to doubt his love but a measure of it, and a summons to run to Christ and to warn others.

Where Christians differ: is punishment eternal, or do the wicked cease to exist? Annihilationists hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist; universalists that all are eventually saved. Some evangelicals hold the first view, pointing to Scripture’s language of destruction, out of reverence for the Bible, not to escape it. This commentary’s view: Jude speaks of eternal chains and eternal fire (vv. 6–7) and utter darkness reserved forever (v. 13). Jesus used the same word, eternal, for both punishment and life (Matthew 25:46). Scripture teaches conscious, eternal punishment for those who reject God (Revelation 14:11; 20:10). This truth is held with sorrow and with urgency to warn and to rescue (v. 23).

Uncertain wording. “Unnatural desire” translates sarkos heteras, literally other flesh, and which “other” Jude means is not certain. It may be flesh of a different kind: the visitors were angels, though the men did not know it, so Sodom crossed from below the line the angels of verse 6 crossed from above. Or it may be desire contrary to God’s design, men pursuing men (Genesis 19:5). The phrase may well cover both; either way Jude names sexual sin that crossed a boundary God had set.

Textual note. In verse 5 the manuscripts differ: some have “the Lord”, others “Jesus”, others “God”. “Jesus” has strong early support and is probably original, since copyists were more likely to change it to “the Lord” than to bring Jesus into an Old Testament scene.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The intruders are walking the road those examples warned against, and it ends in the same darkness. Trusting their dreams, they excuse immorality, contempt for authority and scorn of spiritual powers (v. 8), where even the archangel Michael left judgment to God (v. 9); and the appetites they live by destroy them (v. 10). They follow Cain, Balaam and Korah (v. 11). Five pictures from nature, from hidden reefs and rainless clouds to wandering stars, show people who promise nourishment and guidance and give nothing, or worse (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Portrait of False Teachers

Where even the archangel left judgment to the Lord, these men speak with contempt about what they do not understand.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They shared the church’s love feasts while feeding only themselves.

Now: Beware teaching that looks impressive and spiritual but leaves people no closer to Christ and no more holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With those judgments in plain view, the intruders repeat the same sins: trusting their own dreams, they defile their bodies, throw off the Lord’s authority and speak with contempt of angelic powers.

Yet in like manner. With the examples of verses 5–7 before them, these people do the same things: they defile the flesh, as Sodom did; they reject authority, as unbelieving Israel and the angels did; and they blaspheme the glorious ones. “These people” (houtoi) is Jude’s refrain (vv. 10, 12, 16, 19): each time he turns from the Old Testament examples to the intruders who have “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4).

Relying on their dreams. “Relying on their dreams” (enypniazomenoi) is claiming visions and revelations as authority for their teaching and conduct. It is an old problem: false prophets said, “I have dreamed”, and God answered that they prophesied the deceit of their own heart (Jeremiah 23:25–32). The claim is still heard, “God told me directly”, offered as a reason to set aside what God has revealed publicly and permanently. The dreams come first because they are the source of the three sins that follow: a man who believes he has private revelation feels free to set aside God’s moral law, the Lord’s authority and the unseen world, because he answers to his own visions.

Defile the flesh. This is sexual immorality, the sin of Sodom just named (v. 7): these teachers taught grace as permission (v. 4). In a Greek city where sexual freedom was taken for granted, a Christianity that made no claim on the body would have been welcome, and it still is.

Reject authority. The word (kyriotēs) means lordship, built on kyrios, Lord. Most take it of the Lord’s own authority: they “deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (v. 4), if not in words, then by refusing his rule over how they live. It probably includes the authority of the apostles and church leaders too (v. 17), which they resented as Korah did (v. 11).

Blaspheme the glorious ones. “Glorious ones” (doxas) are almost certainly angelic beings, as in 2 Peter 2:10–11 (see “Uncertain wording” below). Whichever angels are meant, the root is the same: people who think themselves spiritually advanced treat the unseen world as beneath them.

Someone tells me God gave them a dream or a word for me. How should I respond? Kindly, but with Scripture in hand. This commentary holds, charitably toward brothers who differ, that new revelatory gifts ceased with the apostles, because Scripture calls the apostles and prophets the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), laid once, and Jude says the faith was delivered once for all (v. 3). Many charismatic believers agree that any word today must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it. Either way, no dream or word may contradict Scripture, add to the faith once delivered, or override plain obedience. If it agrees with the Bible, you need the Bible, not the dream, to know it is true; if it disagrees, set it aside, however sincere the person. And be especially wary of any claimed revelation that excuses sin, demands money, or puts a leader beyond question; that is exactly what Jude describes.

Uncertain wording. Which angels are meant, and why would anyone speak against them? Some think the intruders mocked the good angels, through whom the law was believed to have been given (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2), so that sneering at angels was sneering at the moral law. Others think they spoke with contempt of evil powers, boasting that the spiritual man has nothing to fear from them. Verse 9, where even Michael will not speak insultingly to the devil, fits this second reading well, and it is the likelier one.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Michael, the mightiest of the angels, would not pass sentence on the devil in his own name but left it to God, so the intruders’ contempt for spiritual powers is pride, not courage.

The archangel Michael. “Archangel” means chief angel, and Michael is the only angel Scripture calls by that title. He stands guard over God’s people (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1) and leads heaven’s armies against the dragon (Revelation 12:7).

The body of Moses. The dispute comes not from the Old Testament but from Jewish tradition (see the textual note below). Deuteronomy says only that God buried Moses and that “no one knows the place of his burial to this day” (Deuteronomy 34:6). In one form of the tradition the devil claimed the body, accusing Moses of murder (Exodus 2:12) as though he were unfit for an honourable burial, and Michael was sent to bury him.

He did not presume. “A blasphemous judgment” is an insulting, slanderous verdict. Michael, mighty as he was, left judgment to God: “The Lord rebuke you” (compare Zechariah 3:2, where the angel of the LORD says the same to Satan). The point is not that the devil deserves respect, but that judgment belongs to God. That contrast is why Jude tells the story. The false teachers sneered at spiritual powers they did not understand (v. 8); Michael understood them far better, had far more authority, and did not. Their contempt is not courage but ignorance and pride.

The Lord who rebukes the devil. The archangel would not pronounce judgment, but he knew who would: the Lord. In the Gospels that Lord stands on earth, saying, “Be gone, Satan!” (Matthew 4:10), and rebuking unclean spirits with a word (Mark 1:25). In Revelation the accuser is thrown down and the saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:7–11). The authority to judge the devil, which the false teachers grabbed and the archangel declined, belongs to Christ, and at the cross he used it to defeat him.

Should Christians rebuke the devil, then? Even the archangel did not pronounce judgment on him in his own authority, but left it to God. Believers are to resist the devil by faith, God’s word and prayer (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–18), not to mock him, address him with bravado or claim authority to bind him. The battle is the Lord’s.

Textual note. Jude draws here, and in verses 14–15, on Jewish traditions that are not in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers such as Origen said that this story came from a book called the Assumption (or Testament) of Moses, whose ending is now lost. Quoting or alluding to a writing does not make that writing Scripture; Paul quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Because Jude wrote by the Spirit, the particular point he cites is true.
verseByVerse.note: The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it was known from Jewish tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The intruders sneer at spiritual realities they cannot grasp, and the only things they do grasp, their animal appetites, are destroying them. Arrogance born of ignorance: the less they know, the more freely they speak.

All that they do not understand. “Blaspheme” here means to speak abusively. They mock what lies beyond them: the unseen world, the holiness of God, the seriousness of judgment.

Like unreasoning animals. “Understand instinctively” (physikōs) means by nature, the way an animal knows food, mating and comfort (2 Peter 2:12). There is a grim irony here: the men who claimed superior spiritual knowledge lived by the knowledge an animal has, and that knowledge, their unchecked appetite, is what destroys them. Paul says the same of those whose “god is their belly” (Philippians 3:19): appetite promises life and delivers ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude pronounces woe on the intruders because they follow three famous rebels, Cain, Balaam and Korah, and so are heading for the same ruin. Each of the three was religious, each led others astray, and each came to judgment.

Woe to them! “Woe” is a prophet’s announcement of judgment, spoken with grief, as in Jesus’ woes on the Pharisees (Matthew 23). Notice the three verbs: they “walked”, they “abandoned themselves”, they “perished”: a way of life, then a headlong plunge, then ruin.

The way of Cain. Cain came to God in his own way and killed the brother whose offering God accepted (Genesis 4; 1 John 3:12): religion on one’s own terms, turning into hatred of the righteous. Later Jewish tradition remembered Cain as the man who said there was no judgment and no judge, which fits teachers who lived as though grace had abolished judgment.

Balaam’s error. Balaam stands for greed: a man to whom God had truly spoken, who put himself up for hire (Numbers 22–24; 2 Peter 2:15). “Abandoned themselves” is literally poured themselves out, rushed headlong: not a slip but a plunge. His counsel led Israel to sexual sin with the women of Moab and to their idol feasts (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16), so that they would “eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality” (Revelation 2:14). Greed and immorality together: exactly the mixture Jude describes.

Korah’s rebellion. Korah stands for rebellion against God’s appointed leaders, for which the earth swallowed him (Numbers 16). His argument sounded spiritual: “all in the congregation are holy, every one of them” (Numbers 16:3), so why should Moses and Aaron lead? Rejecting authority (v. 8) often wears that disguise. “Perished” is past tense: their end is so certain that Jude speaks of it as done. Hatred, greed and proud rebellion: Jude sees all three at once in the men at the love feasts.

In everyday life. In the places where you lead, at home, at work, in a small group, are you feeding others or feeding yourself? Is there any of Cain’s envy, Balaam’s love of gain, or Korah’s resentment of authority in you? Name it before God today; he exposes it in order to forgive it (1 John 1:9).
verseByVerse.note: Cain, Balaam and Korah stand for murderous hatred, greed and rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The intruders sit at the church’s own table as hidden dangers and empty promises: shepherds who feed themselves, clouds without rain, trees without fruit.

Hidden reefs at your love feasts. Five pictures from nature begin here (vv. 12–13). “Hidden reefs” (spilades) are rocks below the water, on which ships are wrecked (see “Uncertain wording” below). “Love feasts” (agapais) were the church’s shared meals, often joined with the Lord’s Supper, where rich and poor, slave and free ate at one table (compare 1 Corinthians 11:20–22). A reef looks like calm water until the hull tears open.

Shepherds feeding themselves. “Without fear” (aphobōs) is without reverence, at the very table where Christ’s death was remembered. Shepherds feeding themselves are the exact opposite of a pastor’s calling (Ezekiel 34:2, 8): shepherds exist to feed the flock, not to feed from it.

Waterless clouds. Clouds that promise rain but give none: so is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give (Proverbs 25:14). In a dry land, clouds on the horizon meant hope; these raise hope and give nothing. “Swept along by winds”: they have no weight of their own and go wherever the latest wind blows, “carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14).

Fruitless trees. Trees that should bear fruit but have none. “Late autumn” is the end of the harvest season, the very time fruit is looked for (Matthew 7:17–19). “Twice dead, uprooted”: as Jesus said, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up” (Matthew 15:13).

How can I tell whether a church leader is feeding the flock or himself? Watch what he does with Scripture, people, money and correction. A true shepherd opens the word faithfully and points to Christ, not himself. He knows and cares for ordinary members, especially the weak and the troubled. He is open about money and does not live off the flock lavishly. He welcomes accountability and can be corrected. A self-feeding shepherd is the reverse: his sermons centre on himself, he courts the influential, he is evasive about finances, and he punishes those who question him. Where a leader abuses people, it must be brought into the light and the victims protected; Christ’s sheep are not his to use.

Uncertain wording. Spilades usually means hidden reefs, but it can also mean stains, and Peter, describing the same people, writes of “blots and blemishes … while they feast with you” (2 Peter 2:13). “Reefs” fits Jude’s run of pictures from sea and sky, and either way the danger sits at the church’s table. “Twice dead” is also uncertain: dead in fruitlessness and dead with roots torn up, or spiritually dead now and destined for the second death (Revelation 20:14). Either way, nothing is left to hope for from such a tree.

verseByVerse.quote: wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The intruders are all noise and no good, like wild waves, and they lead people astray, like wandering stars; and the darkness awaiting them is certain.

Wild waves. Restless, raging, leaving filthy foam and debris on the beach, like the wicked in Isaiah 57:20, whose waters toss up mire and dirt. All energy, and only rubbish left behind.

Wandering stars. “Wandering stars” (asteres planētai) are planets or shooting stars. Sailors navigated by the fixed stars; a star that wanders leads them astray, as the teacher who will not hold the apostolic faith misleads those trying to find the way. In 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes in verse 14, stars that left their appointed courses picture angels who disobeyed and are bound in darkness (1 Enoch 18:13–16; 21:1–6), tying this image back to verse 6.

Reserved forever. “The gloom of utter darkness” echoes the “gloomy darkness” in which the rebel angels are kept (v. 6): the teachers will share their fate. Those who would not shine with a steady light will lose all light.

Five pictures, one diagnosis. The five images come from sea, sky and land, and each is a broken promise: a reef that looks like calm water, a cloud that looks like rain, a tree that looks like harvest, a wave that looks like power, a star that looks like a guide. Each delivers nothing, or worse. That is what false teaching is.

The rock on which no one is wrecked. Against every image of failure stands Christ: the rock on which no one is wrecked, the living water that never runs dry, the true vine, the Lord who stills the waves, the bright morning star. Cain killed his brother; Christ died for his brothers. Balaam sold his gift; Christ gave himself freely. Korah grasped at authority; Christ, who had all authority, took the form of a servant. He is the Good Shepherd who feeds the sheep and lays down his life for them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The judgment of such people was foretold long ago, and the Lord who will carry it out is coming. Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day, without saying the book is Scripture: the Lord comes with countless holy ones to convict the ungodly of every ungodly deed and word (vv. 14–15), a message that matches the rest of the Bible (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31). Then Jude names what marks these men: grumbling, lust, boasting and flattery for gain (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prophecy of Enoch

The Lord will come with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers grumbled, boasted and flattered people for gain.

Now: A true shepherd says what people need to hear; a false one says what pays.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enoch’s ancient prophecy of the Lord coming with his angels to convict the ungodly is about these men too, and their grumbling, lust, boasting and flattery show that it fits them.

Enoch, the seventh from Adam. Enoch walked with God and was taken (Genesis 5:18–24; Hebrews 11:5); with Elijah, he is one of two people in Scripture who did not die. “Seventh from Adam”, counting Adam as the first, is a description found in 1 Enoch itself. Before the flood this man was already warning of the Lord’s coming. Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a prophecy perhaps preserved by tradition from Enoch himself.

Ten thousands of his holy ones. “Comes” (ēlthen) is literally came: the future spoken of as past, because it is as certain as if already done. “Ten thousands” (myriasin) is myriads, an uncountable multitude, and “holy ones” are angels (Deuteronomy 33:2; Matthew 25:31). The sheer number tells of a judgment no one can resist.

To convict all the ungodly. “Convict” (elenxai) is a legal word: to prove guilty so plainly that even the guilty cannot deny it. “Ungodly” comes four times in one sentence: their whole character is ungodliness.

Harsh things. “Harsh things” (sklērōn) are hard, defiant words. God judges words as well as deeds (Matthew 12:36–37). Every careless sneer at God, every mocking word against his Christ, is heard and recorded.

Grumblers, malcontents. “Grumblers” (gongystai) are murmurers, like Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10); the word sounds like a low discontented muttering. “Malcontents” (mempsimoiroi) are complainers about their lot, who always find something wrong with what God has given them. Their complaints and their lusts are connected: a heart that will not be content with God’s provision goes looking for its own.

Loud-mouthed boasters. “Loud-mouthed” (hyperonka) is swelling, bombastic, as in 2 Peter 2:18. Big words, little substance.

Admiring faces. “Showing favoritism” (thaumazontes prosōpa) is literally admiring faces: flattering the influential for profit (James 2:1–9). They said what their audience wanted to hear and were rewarded for it. Grumbling about God, they fawn over people who can pay.

The coming Lord has a name. In 1 Enoch the one who comes is God. Jude, who has just called Jesus our only Master and Lord (v. 4), most likely understands the coming Lord to be the risen Jesus: the Son of Man will come in his glory, and all the angels with him (Matthew 25:31), for the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The brother Jude once did not believe is the Judge before whom every harsh word will be answered for. And yet this same Lord, before he comes in glory, came in humility: the Judge stood in the dock, was convicted in our place, and bore the sentence. So the day that will expose the ungodly holds no terror for those who are hidden in him.

In everyday life. Watch for grumbling in your own heart this week. Each time you catch yourself complaining, about the weather, the boss, the church, stop and name one specific gift of God instead, and ask the Spirit to teach you the contentment Paul learned in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13).

Is 1 Enoch Scripture, then? Jude says that Enoch truly prophesied this. Some think Jude regarded the book as inspired; more likely he affirms this one prophecy as true without endorsing the whole book (see “Where Christians differ” below). A true statement is true wherever it is found, and the Holy Spirit led Jude to use this one.

Is grumbling really that serious? Scripture treats it as far more serious than we do. Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness was counted as unbelief and rebellion (Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). Grumbling says that God has given me less than I deserve and is not managing my life well. It poisons fellowship, spreads quickly, and is often the first sign of a heart drifting from God. The remedy is not pretending all is well, for the psalms are full of honest lament, but thankfulness and contentment (Philippians 2:14; 4:11–13). Lament takes the pain to God; grumbling talks about God behind his back.

How do I tell flattery from genuine encouragement? Encouragement tells the truth in love for the other person’s good; flattery tells pleasing untruths for the flatterer’s good. Encouragement is specific and honest and, when needed, includes correction (Proverbs 27:6). Flattery is vague and excessive, aimed especially at those with power or money, and never risks a hard word. Be careful of anyone who only ever tells you what you want to hear. When you encourage others, give thanks for real evidences of grace in them, and be just as ready to say a difficult word gently. Giving flattery and enjoying it feed the same hunger, to be thought well of; a heart that already rests in God’s favour in Christ does not need to buy favour, and is much harder to buy.

Where Christians differ: does quoting 1 Enoch make it Scripture? The Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes 1 Enoch in its canon. This commentary’s view: Jude quotes one prophecy from 1 Enoch and affirms it as true, as Paul quoted true statements from pagan poets; this does not make the whole book inspired. Jesus and the apostles never treat 1 Enoch as Scripture, the Jewish people did not include it in the Hebrew Scriptures, and the church at large, though a few early writers valued it, did not receive it; it also contains much that is legendary. The canon is closed and does not include it.
verseByVerse.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time. Quoting it does not make it Scripture; Paul also quoted pagan poets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers answer false teaching not with panic but with memory, growth and mercy. The apostles foretold such scoffers, so their arrival should shake no one (vv. 17–19). The faithful are to keep themselves in God’s love by building on the faith, praying in the Spirit and waiting for Christ’s mercy (vv. 20–21). Their own life in God comes first, and from there they reach out to rescue others: patient with doubters, urgent with those near the fire, merciful yet careful with those stained by sin (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
But You, Beloved

On keeping yourselves in God’s love, and on the rescue of others, see the note on vv. 20–23.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles had foretold scoffers in the last time.

Now: Meet each person where they are: patience for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and care for yourself in the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles foretold that mockers would come, living by their own desires and splitting the church, so their arrival should not shake believers: they are what was predicted, and they do not have the Spirit.

Remember the predictions. Here the letter turns from the false teachers to the people Jude loves. “Predictions” (rhēmatōn) are words spoken beforehand. Paul warned that fierce wolves would come in (Acts 20:29–30) and that some would depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1); Peter warned of scoffers (2 Peter 3:3). Whoever knows that false teaching was foretold is less likely to be shaken when it arrives: the danger was on the map.

Scoffers. “Last time” is the whole period since Christ’s coming. “Scoffers” (empaiktai) are mockers, as in 2 Peter 3:3. Their teaching serves their way of life: they decide first how they want to live, and then shape their doctrine to excuse it.

Cause divisions. “Cause divisions” (apodiorizontes) is make separations. Perhaps they claimed to be a spiritual elite, with the dreams and the higher knowledge, above ordinary believers.

Worldly people. “Worldly” (psychikoi) is natural, unspiritual (1 Corinthians 2:14; James 3:15): living by mere human nature, as people never born again. They had religion, but everything about them could be explained without God.

Devoid of the Spirit. Literally not having the Spirit (pneuma mē echontes). This is the decisive mark, and Jude says it last: they are not Christians at all (Romans 8:9). The one thing they most loudly claim is the thing they most plainly lack. Where the Spirit’s fruit is love, joy and peace (Galatians 5:22–23), theirs is division, loose living, grumbling and self-promotion.

I have told you beforehand. Behind the apostles stands their Lord, who warned that false christs and false prophets would arise, and then said, “See, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew 24:24–25). So scoffers are no sign that Christ has lost control of his church; they fulfil his word. And the Lord who saw the danger coming has also said that the gates of hell will not prevail against his church (Matthew 16:18).

How do I know whether I have the Spirit? Every true believer has the Spirit; there is no second class of Christians who lack him (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). The evidence is not dramatic experience but his ordinary work: you confess Jesus as Lord from the heart (1 Corinthians 12:3); you cry to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16); you love Christ and his word; you fight sin and want holiness; you love other believers; and his fruit is growing in you, however slowly. If you see these, however faintly, the Spirit is at work. If you do not, ask, for God gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Is every division in the church caused by people like this? No. Some separations are necessary, when the gospel itself is denied (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10). Many divisions among true believers come from ordinary sin, misunderstanding or honest disagreement on secondary matters, as between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). Jude’s divisive people split the church around themselves, claiming higher spirituality, while living for their own desires. Before you separate from other believers, ask whether the issue is the gospel or your preference, and whether you have truly sought peace.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to keep themselves in God’s love by building on the faith, praying in the Spirit and waiting for Christ’s mercy, and from there to reach out with mercy to rescue those being drawn away. The one command is “keep yourselves in the love of God”; building, praying and waiting are how it is done.

Building yourselves up. “Building up” (epoikodomountes) is construction on the foundation of the apostolic faith, “most holy” because it comes from God (v. 3): growing in Scripture and sound doctrine (Colossians 2:7; Acts 20:32). The word is plural: this is done together, as a church.

Praying in the Holy Spirit. Prayer guided and empowered by the Spirit, according to God’s will (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18), so that our prayer comes into line with his own praying for us. The Spirit whom the scoffers lack (v. 19) helps believers pray. (On whether this means praying in tongues, see “Where Christians differ” at the end of this note.)

Keep yourselves in the love of God. The main command. “Keep” (tērēsate) is guard, preserve, echoing verse 1 (kept for Jesus Christ) and verse 6 (the angels who did not keep their position). Jude does not say, “Make God love you”; that is settled (v. 1). He says, stay where that love is known and enjoyed (John 15:9–10), as a man stays by the fire on a cold night. And we stay there imperfectly. The Son kept his Father’s commandments and abides in his love without fault, and he did it for us. We stand before God on his obedience, not ours.

Waiting for the mercy. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi) is eagerly expecting. “Mercy” is the mercy Christ will show at his return, the mercy of verse 2 awaited in its fullest form. Even at the judgment, believers look for mercy, not for wages they have earned. Note the Trinity: Spirit, Father and Lord Jesus Christ, all in two verses.

Those who doubt. The rescue has three groups who need different help. “Those who doubt” are believers unsettled by the false teachers (see “Uncertain wording” below). They need patient compassion, not condemnation.

Snatching them out of the fire. “Snatching” (harpazontes) is seizing quickly: those on the edge of destruction need urgent rescue, as from a burning building, like the brand (a burning stick) plucked from the burning (Amos 4:11).

Mercy with fear. The most deeply corrupted still receive mercy, but with caution, lest you be dragged down too (Galatians 6:1). “Garment stained” (spilōmenon chitōna) is a soiled undergarment, a life made dirty by sin (compare Zechariah 3:3–4), and “the flesh” is our sinful nature. Show the person mercy, but keep clear of the sin.

A brand plucked from the fire. Jude’s pictures of rescue echo Zechariah 3, where Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments with Satan accusing him. The LORD rebukes Satan and asks, “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?” The filthy garments are taken away, and God promises to remove iniquity in a single day (Zechariah 3:1–9). That day came at the cross, where Christ was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). Every believer is a brand snatched from the fire, and that is why we go to others with mercy.

If God keeps us, why are we told to keep ourselves in the love of God? Both are true (vv. 1, 24): God keeps his people through their keeping themselves, building up their faith, praying and waiting for Christ’s mercy. Our effort is the means of his keeping, not a rival to it (Philippians 2:12–13), which is why Jude can end with full confidence in him who is able to keep you from stumbling.

How do I keep myself in the love of God? Through the three activities around the command, each of them ordinary. Start where you are loved. Each morning, before the day tells you what you are worth, remind yourself what verse 1 says you already are: called, “beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ”. Build on the faith, together. Read a passage slowly, ask what it shows you of Christ, and talk about it with another believer; love is best enjoyed by those who keep hearing it described. Pray in the Spirit. Turn what you have read into prayer, and bring him the day’s fears and sins as they come instead of saving them up. Wait for mercy. When you fail, do not step out of the warmth to punish yourself; look ahead to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, which you are waiting for, not earning. You do not stay in his love by holding on harder, but by staying near the fire he lit at the cross, where the Son was forsaken so that you never will be (Mark 15:34).

A friend is doubting. What do I actually do? Start with mercy, as Jude says. Listen before you answer, and find out what the doubt really is: intellectual, moral or born of suffering. Do not be shocked or impatient, and share your own struggles where it helps. Point to Christ himself more than to arguments: read a Gospel together, or a psalm of lament. Offer a good book if the question is intellectual, but stay with them; doubt is often lonely. Pray for them and with them, keep them in the fellowship of the church, and be patient: many doubters come through to a stronger faith.

How do I help someone caught in sin without being pulled in myself? Go humbly, aware that you could fall too (Galatians 6:1). Do not go alone when the sin is one that tempts you; take a mature believer, and do not linger in the places or conversations where the sin lives. Keep your own walk with God close through prayer, Scripture and accountability. Speak clearly about the sin and warmly about Christ. If the person is unrepentant and the sin serious, involve the church’s elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Mercy is the goal; fear is the guard.

Where Christians differ: does “praying in the Holy Spirit” mean praying in tongues? Some charismatic believers take it as speaking in tongues. Many who pray in this way are earnest believers who love Christ; the question here is only what Jude meant. This commentary’s view: Nothing in the context mentions tongues. Praying in the Spirit means praying under the Spirit’s guidance and in dependence on him, according to God’s will revealed in his word (Ephesians 6:18). All believers can and should pray this way.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “those who doubt” (diakrinomenous) usually means to doubt or waver in the New Testament (James 1:6), but it can also mean to dispute, as in verse 9, where Michael was “disputing” with the devil; so some translate it as those who argue, to be answered and convinced. “Doubt” is the likelier meaning, since Jude calls for mercy towards them; either way they are to be won, not written off.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ in verses 22–23, some describing two groups, others three. The ESV follows the three-group reading, which has good early support; the King James Version, following later manuscripts, has two groups (“of some have compassion, making a difference: and others save with fear”).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends in adoration, because the safety of God’s people rests finally on God. After so many examples of those who fell, Jude lifts our eyes to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and to present them blameless before his glory with great joy (v. 24). To him, through Jesus Christ, belong glory and authority for ever (v. 25). The doxology is the ground on which the whole letter stands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Him Who Is Able

Perseverance rests on God’s ability, not ours (see the note on vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was pointed to God’s glory, majesty, dominion and authority.

Now: The same God holds his people through every crisis, and will bring them home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude ends by giving all glory, for all time, to the only God, who through Jesus Christ is able to keep his people from falling and bring them blameless and rejoicing into his presence.

Him who is able. “Able” (dynamenō) is has the power: God is not merely willing to keep his people; he is able. In a letter full of people who fell, this changes everything. Whatever you fear, stumbling, lost ground, false teaching that might overwhelm you, the One who keeps you is stronger: he spoke creation into being and holds it together by his word. “From stumbling” (aptaistous) is sure-footed, like a horse that does not stumble, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament. He is not a safety net at the bottom of the cliff but a shepherd on the path, keeping the feet of his sheep.

Blameless with great joy. “Present” (stēsai) is cause to stand, the language of formal presentation before a king. “Blameless” (amōmous) is without blemish, the word for a sacrifice without defect (Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22). “Great joy” (agalliasis) is exultation, God’s and ours: the joy of the father running to meet his returning son (Luke 15:20). The homecoming of the saints is a joy to God.

The only God, our Savior. “Our Saviour” is used of the Father here, as in 1 Timothy 1:1; more often the title belongs to Jesus. The salvation Christ accomplished is the Father’s salvation, and all glory is given to God through Christ. With the Spirit named in the praying (v. 20), Father, Son and Spirit are all here.

Glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. “Glory” (doxa) is the weight and radiance of God’s being; “majesty” (megalōsynē) his sovereign greatness; “dominion” (kratos) his power over all created things; “authority” (exousia) the right to rule. The false teachers rejected authority (v. 8); here all authority is ascribed to God.

Before all time. Before creation he was glorious; now, with false teachers in the church, he is glorious; and when every believer who feared stumbling is presented blameless, he will be glorious for ever. The letter that began with an alarm ends with the God who was never alarmed, and with the words “him who is able”. That is enough to carry a stumbling church to glory, through every danger and every fall, until his people stand before his throne without blemish, with exultation, his and theirs together.

Blameless because he was spotless. Blameless is the language of sacrifice, and it is used of one sacrifice above all: Christ offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 1:19). That is how stumbling sinners can stand faultless in the presence of glory: the spotlessness they will wear is first his. And the joy of the presentation is his too, for it was for the joy set before him that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

In everyday life. Learn this doxology by heart, and say it when you feel weakest: when you have fallen, when you fear you will, when the news about the church is bad. Let the last word in your mind be his ability, not your inability, and pray it over a struggling believer by name.

Will I really be blameless? I know how much I still sin. Yes, and not because you will one day manage it yourself. Christ gave himself up for his church to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). His blood has already cleansed you of guilt, and at his coming he will complete your sanctification: you will be like him, for you will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Justification declared you righteous once and for all; sanctification, the Spirit’s work of making you actually holy, begun at your new birth and growing now, will be finished then. There is no purgatory to pass through; the finished work of Christ is enough. Your present sin should make you humble and watchful, but not hopeless: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

What if I am afraid that I will fall away? The fear itself, if it drives you to Christ, is a mercy. But your security does not rest on the strength of your grip; it rests on his. Jude does not say “to him who hopes you will manage”, but “to him who is able”. Christ prays for you (Hebrews 7:25), the Father holds you (John 10:29), and the Spirit seals you (Ephesians 1:13–14). So use the means Jude gave (vv. 20–21), and then rest. A child carried across a river is not safe because of how tightly he holds on, but because of the arms that hold him.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.<sup>3</sup>Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.<sup>4</sup>For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.<sup>5</sup>Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.<sup>6</sup>And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day—<sup>7</sup>just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.<sup>8</sup>Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.<sup>9</sup>But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.”<sup>10</sup>But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively.<sup>11</sup>Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion.<sup>12</sup>These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted;<sup>13</sup>wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.<sup>14</sup>It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, “Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones,<sup>15</sup>to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”<sup>16</sup>These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.<sup>17</sup>But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>They said to you, “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.”<sup>19</sup>It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.<sup>20</sup>But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,<sup>21</sup>keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.<sup>22</sup>And have mercy on those who doubt;<sup>23</sup>save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.<sup>24</sup>Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy,<sup>25</sup>to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.

keyVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.
keyVerse.note: Here Jude says why he wrote. The faith is not a theory still developing but a gospel God has handed to his people complete, and when it is threatened every believer is called to defend it. The rest of the letter shows why it must be defended and how, and its closing doxology shows who keeps the defenders (vv. 24–25).

1.reflection:
Jude tells his readers that they are called, beloved and kept (v. 1) before he warns them of anything. Why do you think he begins there? How does knowing you are held change the way you face danger, temptation or bad news?

The intruders turned “the grace of our God into sensuality” (v. 4). In what ways is grace treated as an excuse for sin today, around us or in our own hearts? How does true grace answer this (Titus 2:11–12)?

Jude pictures false teachers as reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves and wandering stars (vv. 12–13). What does each picture teach about recognising teaching that promises much and gives nothing? Where have you seen it?

Verses 20–23 tell us to keep ourselves in God’s love and to show mercy to doubters and to those caught in sin. Who in your life is doubting or drifting, and what would it look like this week to show them mercy without being drawn in yourself?
